stories.title: More hosepipe bans in force as drought declared - is your area affected?
stories.summary: Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales are under drought conditions, with repeated heatwaves leaving water supplies under strain. Both England and Wales provisionally recorded their driest July on record. This lack of rainfall - on top of hot, dry weather in spring and early summer - has taken its toll on rivers, crops and nature. Roughly 30 million people across parts of England and Wales are now covered by hosepipe bans. So how is your area doing and are you in a drought? There is no single definition of drought, but it is characterised by a period of low rainfall. As the ground dries out, crops and vegetation can begin to struggle. If dry conditions persist, rivers, reservoirs and groundwater levels can also fall, putting pressure on water supplies. Environmental bodies in each UK nation decide whether to declare drought or water scarcity by assessing current water resources alongside weather forecasts. Both drought and water scarcity can lead to hosepipe bans, if they are not already in place. While drought is driven by prolonged dry weather, water scarcity occurs when demand for water outstrips the available supply. This summer, restrictions have been introduced in some areas to help manage high demand.

stories.title: One still missing after Grand Canyon floods kill two and prompts rescue efforts
stories.summary: All but one person missing after flash flooding devastated parts of the Grand Canyon has now been found, the National Parks Service (NPS) says. Thirty people had previously been unaccounted for, but rangers "worked tirelessly" to reduce that number, Incident Commander Dave Black told reporters on Monday. At least two people died after floodwaters struck on Saturday afternoon, wiping out footbridges and propelling boulders downstream. Crews had "worked incredibly hard trying to get this situation under control", Black said during Monday's press conference. This involved the airlift of dozens of people in Phantom Ranch, one of the park's hardest-hit areas, he added. An initial 45 people were evacuated by air on Saturday, and a remaining group of 37 were later evacuated by Sunday afternoon, Black said. "We've had a very busy couple of days," the official added. Crews will be deployed on Tuesday morning to search for the final missing person in the area between Phantom Ranch and Cottonwood Manzanita. Further heavy rain was forecast overnight from Monday into Tuesday, bringing an elevated risk of additional flash flooding to the area. Black described the two individuals who died as adult males, adding he would not disclose any further details about their identities. The NPS earlier said it had found the body of a 46-year-old man near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River. The "significant" flooding began in Bright Angel Canyon around 14:30 local time (19:30 BST) on Saturday, the NPS previously said.

stories.title: Iran has no nuclear production at Mount Kuh-e Kolang Gaz-La — Foreign Ministry
stories.summary: Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei highlighted that IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi is aware of this position
article_sentences: TEHRAN, September 1.

Iran is not engaged in uranium enrichment activities at Mount Kuh-e Kolang Gaz-La, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said, adding that IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi is aware of this position.
"The words of the director general themselves demonstrate the truthfulness of our statements: we have no nuclear activities at Mount Kuh-e Kolang Gaz-La," he said at a briefing.
According to Baghaei, Iran is in contact with the IAEA, but there are currently no talks on the Iranian nuclear program.

Baghaei previously said that US President Donald Trump’s statements about Iran’s alleged new nuclear facility are unfounded, and Washington’s obsessive attention to Mount Kuh-e Kolang Gaz·La, where no nuclear activity is taking place, is nothing more than a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage.

stories.title: Russia granted exclusive right to continue ocean exploration in Pacific
stories.summary: The area where Russia is conducting the exploration for mineral resources covers 75,000 square kilometers
article_sentences: MOSCOW, September 1.

Russia's exclusive right to explore polymetallic nodules in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone of the northeastern Pacific Ocean has been extended until 2031, the Russian Ministry of Natural Resources announced.
The relevant contract was extended by Yuzhmorgeologiya and the International Seabed Authority (ISA).
It was signed on behalf of the ISA by Secretary-General Michael Lodge.
Following a visit to Moscow, he will participate in the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok, the ministry noted.
The area where Russia is conducting the exploration for mineral resources covers 75,000 square kilometers.

Polymetallic nodules in the Pacific Ocean are located at depths ranging from 4.7 to 5.4 kilometers, containing nickel, cobalt, manganese, and rare-earth elements, the Russian Ministry of Natural Resources noted.
"These are crucial components.
For instance, cobalt and manganese are used in metallurgy to improve steel quality.
These metals are also 'battery metals,' meaning they are used in the manufacture of various types of electric vehicles.
Copper, meanwhile, is the third most in-demand metal in the world, after iron and aluminum.
It is essential for the production of computers, televisions, and microwave ovens; it is used in drinking water supply systems and serves as a component in parts for aircraft, trains, and ships.
